newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cuba to ratify chemical arms treaty, UN says.
newsitem.headline: Cuba to ratify chemical arms treaty, UN says.

text.p: Cuba intends to submit its ratification papers for the chemical weapons treaty on Monday, the United Nations reported on Saturday.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan, in a statement, said he "welcomes this action and hopes that other nations that have not yet ratified will do so."

On Friday, the United States and China were among seven countries that deposited with the United Nations their instruments of ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention. The others were Bangladesh, Equatorial Guinea, Kenya, Togo and Zimbabwe.
This brings to 81 the number of countries that have so far ratified the treaty. It is designed to outlaw the production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons worldwide.
The convention, which has been signed by 164 countries, enters into force next Tuesday.

American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson deposited the U.S. ratification less than 24 hours after the Senate approved the treaty late on Thursday by a vote of 74 to 26, seven more than the required two-thirds majority.
Other countries that have ratified the accord include Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Japan.
Russia is the only one of the U.N. Security Council's five permanent members that has not yet done so.

U.S. Senate conservatives had criticised the treaty for a variety of reasons, including a provision they said could lead to the United States having to share chemical defence technology with such adversaries as Iran or Cuba.

But administration officials said that only countries that have destroyed their stockpiles can request defensive assistance -- and then only if they are threatened with, or under, chemical attack. President Bill Clinton has told the Senate that the United States will limit its assistance to certain countries, like Cuba, to emergency medical supplies.
